## Chapter 1

On Moran’s promotion Mr. Seward asked whether the Minister would like his son made Assistant Secretary. It was the first—and last—office ever offered him, though, in truth, offered to his father. The change seemed useless. Any young man could make some sort of Assistant Secretary; only one, at that moment, could make an Assistant Son. His duties were half domestic, often required absence, and always independence of the Government service. The British Government by courtesy let him go to Court as Attaché though never attached; after some years the tolerance was declared irregular. In society, when official, he was with the Minister; when unofficial, he was nobody; and he began to find advantages in being nobody—free to aspire only to be a gentleman, and to take from the irregular position an irregular education, the only sort he was to get.

Under danger Mr. Seward learned also. He felt that mere despatches weighed little, and that European opinion must be met by American opinion and interests, personally applied. He sent over every important American he could lay hands on. They all came to the Legation; they worked quietly; the waste seemed great, but it all told in the end, and meanwhile it helped education.

One of these, a political master from New York, took charge of the press, began—amusing the secretaries—by writing to the Times, mistake or not, and soon held the threads and did smoothly all that could be done. He himself was the education: mind strong and balanced; temper unruffled; manners of benevolent simplicity; a model of patient address. Most of all, he seemed unselfish—an immune from the diseased appetite of egotism that power breeds. He grasped power but not office; gave, without caring to take. Management was his instinct; he played with men as with cards, for their face-value, keeping himself in the background. Once, after stories strong even for the Albany lobby, the private secretary asked outright: “Then, do you think that no politician can be trusted?”

“I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so.”

At the time this meant: Youth needs illusions. Later it looked like the rule of play: every card has its relative value; principles are less useful than values. Another visitor, a great advocate sent as law counsel, put it otherwise: “The world can absorb only doses of truth; too much would kill it.” Education should adjust the dose.

England’s power of absorbing truth seemed small. Men like Palmerston and Russell, the Times and the Standard, offered a study that sickened a student with anxiety. He had begun—contrary to advice—by taking their bad faith for granted. Was he wrong? Life changed front according as one dealt with honest men or rogues.

Thus far the Legation, for safety, put little confidence in Ministers. Recognition of belligerency, the Declaration of Paris, the Trent affair—all strengthened belief that Lord Russell started in May, 1861, with the assumption that the Confederacy was established; every step proved persistence; he would never consent to put obstacles in the way of recognition; he was waiting only the proper moment to interpose. These points seemed fixed, save that Russell obstinately denied them and assured the Minister of honest neutrality.

With the insolence of youth, Henry Adams leaped to the conclusion that Russell—like other statesmen—lied, although his father thought otherwise. Then came the stages of the Alabama. After one cruiser’s escape, the Minister remonstrated against the escape of “No. 290.” Russell declined to act. New evidence went in every few days; with it, July 24, Collier’s legal opinion: “It appears difficult to make out a stronger case of infringement of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which, if not enforced on this occasion, is little better than a dead letter.” Four days later the ship escaped.

Young Adams cared little for law as law; he took his law from lawyers. Could one afford to trust human nature in politics? Sir Robert Collier seemed to say that Law agreed with History: trust no mortal man.

Russell felt the force of the inference and spent his life trying to disprove it. He began by blaming the law officers; then, in his Recollections, pleaded guilty to criminal negligence: “I assent entirely to the opinion of the Lord Chief Justice of England that the Alabama ought to have been detained during the four days I was waiting for the opinion of the law officers.... It was my fault as Secretary of State.” Of course it was his fault! The issue lay not in fault but in intent. To a young man, there could be no sense in history unless a constant course of faults implied a constant motive.

For the Minister it was a practical matter; he held, conveniently and to the last, that Russell was true. The son wanted to know whether one could, in politics, risk trusting any one. Argyll believed Russell honest; Westbury, head and heart of the rebel contention, made no such claim, and as far as his authority went affirmed the law that in politics no man should be trusted.

Years later, Spencer Walpole’s Life of Russell told what the Minister never knew. The Alabama escaped July 28, 1862. After the Union disasters and Lee’s invasion, Palmerston instantly wrote, September 14: “If this should happen, would it not be time for us to consider whether... England and France might not address the contending parties and recommend an arrangement on the basis of separation?”

Forty years later, Gladstone's own confession revealed that the Cabinet's drift toward intervention had been even nearer success than Adams had supposed; the lesson stood, that in politics no professed friend in power could be trusted, and that the diplomatic victory of 1862 had been won against men who scarcely knew their own minds.
